Every arrow means one part of the code imports another. Draw them all and you get the project's map.
Reading the graph tells you what is safe to change: arrows show which parts break when another does.
`{repo}` has {components} components joined by {edges} import arrows.
Fan-in counts how many parts import a module. High fan-in means a lot of code leans on it.
Modules with high fan-in should be stable and well tested, because a bug there spreads everywhere.
Fan-out counts how many other parts a module imports. High fan-out means it breaks whenever any of them change.
A module with huge fan-out is often doing too many jobs. Splitting it lowers the risk.
The heart is the file that the most code depends on. Break it and almost everything stops working.
Projects protect their heart with tests and careful reviews, because a change there touches everyone.
The heart of `{repo}` is `{file}`, imported {fanIn} times.
A imports B and B imports A, so neither can be understood, tested or loaded alone. That's a knot in the code.
To fix one, move the shared part into a third module that both import, or pass the dependency in.
{members} import each other in a loop.
`{repo}` has {cycles} import loop(s). Each one is a weak point.
`{component}` is stuck in an import loop.
Coupling is how tangled modules are with each other. Loosely coupled code can change one piece without touching the rest.
Fewer imports between modules and shorter import chains mean lower coupling and easier changes.
A component is a folder of code with one job. Good projects are built from parts with clear borders.
When each component has a single job, you can find bugs faster and swap parts out.
When a module breaks, everything that imports it can break too, like dominoes.
That's why high fan-in modules need tests: one bug there cascades through every dependent.
`{component}` broke, and {dependents} components depend on it.
`{component}` is imported by {fanIn} components, which is why the hit cascaded.
Dead code is code that nothing uses anymore. It still has to be read, compiled and maintained.
Deleting unused code is one of the safest refactors, and version control keeps a copy if you ever need it back.
`{file}` ({loc} lines) just got deleted, and nothing broke.
Every quick hack and TODO is a loan against the future. Like money debt, it piles up interest: slower changes and more bugs.
Teams pay it down a little at a time by fixing TODOs and cleaning up hacks when they touch that code.
Tests are code that checks your code. They catch bugs before your users do, so they act as armor.

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem until it hits a base case.
Every recursion needs a stopping rule. Without one, it runs until the stack overflows.
Each function call stacks a frame in memory. Call too deep, like endless recursion, and the stack overflows and the program crashes.
The fix is a proper base case, or turning deep recursion into a loop.
Two things run at once and touch the same data. Whoever wins the race decides the result, and that changes run to run.
Locks, queues and immutable data stop races. These bugs are hard to reproduce, so they're nasty.
A leak is memory the program grabs and never gives back. It grows and grows until something falls over.
Forgotten listeners, caches with no limit and global lists are classic leaks.
Two people changed the same lines in different ways. Git can't guess who's right, so a human must choose.
Small, frequent commits and talking to teammates keep conflicts rare and small.
`git push --force` overwrites history on the server, and teammates' commits can vanish.
Use `--force-with-lease`, and never force-push a shared branch like main.
Package A needs lib v1, package B needs lib v2, and you can't have both. Welcome to dependency hell.
Lockfiles, fewer dependencies and regular updates keep you out of it.
Code follows a reference that points at nothing, so null crashes the program.
Check for missing values, or use types that force you to (Option, Maybe, strict null checks).
A loop whose exit condition never becomes true runs forever and freezes the program.
Make sure something inside the loop moves toward the exit condition every time.
Refactoring changes how code is organized without changing what it does: cleaner, smaller, easier to read.
Tests make refactoring safe. They prove the behavior stayed the same.

用 print、变量和 f-string 制作个人介绍卡。
零基础；能在课堂编辑器输入并提交代码。
让学生现场修改变量验证输出确实随变量变化，检查是否把变量名写进引号。f-string 可用单引号或双引号；不要按引号风格扣分。
把输入的秒数转换成分钟和秒，理解字符串与整数。
完成 01：变量、print 和基本表达式。
重点检查 int、/、//、% 的差异；不要求本课捕获 ValueError。不要让学生为尚未教过的非法输入处理丢分。
清理空格、统一大小写、替换文本并安全截取预览。
完成 02：读取输入、变量和类型。
先问原字符串是否改变，再实际打印验证。切片接受负索引等合理扩展，但不要把字符串短于 3 当作错误输入。
给分数分等级，练习 if / elif / else 和边界条件。
完成 03；知道整数比较和输入转换。
重点检查范围验证的位置和 >= 与 >。接受等价且正确的写法；示例分数都是整数，不要求处理字母输入。
制作训练计数器：循环、累加和筛选。
完成 04：比较运算与条件分支。
让学生画出每轮 total 的值。接受 += 或等价累加；讲清 range(1, n + 1) 的端点。
做一个有边界的倒计时，再理解 break 与输入哨兵。
完成 05：循环、累加和条件判断。
先手工检查终止条件再运行。遇到无限循环可用 Ctrl+C 中断。明确 attempts 统计读取次数，包括 -1；非整数处理不在本课范围。
建立背包列表，添加物品、遍历并处理空列表。
完成 06；知道字符串、循环和 len。
强调列表可以重复且有顺序，索引从 0 开始。元组仅作序列对比，不要求嵌套可变对象或深入不可变性。
把重复逻辑封装成函数，区分 print 与 return。
完成 07：列表、条件判断和循环。
检查函数每次调用是否重新初始化局部累加值，解释 return 与 print。断言是本地自测；平台不会执行上传代码。
用键值对管理库存，安全查询、更新，并遍历字典。
完成 08；会使用列表、函数、条件和循环。
可直接修改传入字典，不强制复制。检查 .get 的默认值、重复键覆盖、空字典，以及负数入库不应修改数据。不要把字典顺序或单/双引号风格作为功能要求。
建议课时：30 分钟，三个步骤各 10 分钟；可根据班级情况延长。
每步建议：演示 2 分钟 → 独立编码 5 分钟 → 同桌检查 2 分钟 → 提交与集体攻击 1 分钟。
检查范围：预设只检查文件、源码片段与自测记录。文本片段可能出现在注释中，检查通过不代表程序正确。请让学生运行示例并解释结果，再用教师复核记录最终功能分数。接受正确的等价实现；可删除不适用的文本检查，或添加自己仓库的 GitHub CI 检查。
